title: Jamie Dimon Hated Bitcoin: JPMorgan Now Expects BTC to Beat Stocks and Gold - CryptoPotato
content: JPMorgan’s long-term CEO, Jamie Dimon, once called bitcoin a “fraud,” said that it was “worthless,” and described it as a “decentralized Ponzi scheme.” Moreover, he claimed that if he were using the government, he would shut it down. Fast-forward several years, and the banking behemoth he runs is putting traditional finance on public blockchains, accepting BTC and ETH as collateral, and, oh right, predicting that BTC could outperform stocks and gold over the next 10-15 years. One of the first criticisms caught on camera from Dimon dates back to at least 2017, when he called the largest cryptocurrency a “fraud” that would eventually blow up. He added that JPM traders caught dealing with it would be fired and also compared BTC to the infamous tulip bubble. Although he later regretted using the term “fraud,” his hostile stance continued. Four years later, Dimon advised investors to “stay away” from crypto, arguing that the asset class could not compare with fiat currencies or gold. He also described bitcoin as “worthless” and the “fool’s gold of the future.” By 2022, the rhetoric had become even stronger as Dimon described Bitcoin and other digital assets as “decentralized Ponzi schemes.” In 2023, he kept the blows coming, dismissing BTC as a “pet rock.” The same year saw perhaps the most memorable attack. During a Senate hearing, the exec said that if he were running the US government, he would “close it down,” while claiming that cryptocurrencies were heavily associated with criminal activity. Despite all of his criticism and blatant claims, JPMorgan’s business strategy was already moving in a very different direction. The bank launched JPM Coin, built its Onyx blockchain infrastructure, executed tokenized collateral transactions involving BlackRock and Barclays, invested in blockchain intelligence company TRM Labs, and gave wealth-management clients access to crypto funds. The divergence between Dimon’s public comments and JPM’s commercial strategy has become even harder to ignore. The Wall Street behemoth recently let institutional clients use BTC and ETH as collateral for loans, one of its most direct integrations of native crypto assets into conventional banking. It has also worked with Coinbase to make crypto purchases more accessible to Chase customers, while JPMorgan Securities has served as an authorized participant for BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin ETF. On the blockchain side, JPM has expanded into public networks, with JPM Coin (JPMD) now available on Ethereum and Base. The bank has also launched tokenized money-market funds on Ethereum and is expanding JPM Coin to the Canton Network. The winds seem to have shifted after its report last week. Although the bank still believes BTC could be highly volatile, it predicted that the leading cryptocurrency – once referred to as “fraud” and “worthless,” is likely to outperform large-cap stocks, REITs, and gold over the next 10-15 years with a 10% annual compounded return. title: JPMorgan Has Nearly $900 Million in Tokenized Funds on Ethereum and Solana. Which Chain Benefits More? - 24/7 Wall St.

JPMorgan just parked nearly $900 million in tokenized funds across Ethereum and Solana, but the fine print reveals one chain got a much bigger piece of the deal than the headlines suggest. It sounds nuts, but SoFi is giving new Active Invest users up to $1,000 in stock for a limited time, and all it takes is a $50 deposit to get started. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM | JPM Price Prediction) has made headlines by placing nearly $900 million in tokenized funds on both Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL). A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock. According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone. In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%. JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. JPMorgan designed it so that stablecoin issuers can hold reserves in JLTXX tokens under the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law. JPMorgan first launched JLTXX on Ethereum in May. MONY, by contrast, is a private placement regulated under the SEC’s Rule 506(c), meaning only high-net-worth individuals can invest. JPMorgan rolled this fund out in December 2025. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan’s cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. Retail traders cannot purchase these tokens on exchanges. Meanwhile, JPMD is a deposit token representing a dollar held in a JPMorgan bank account, enabling institutional clients to transact at any time. It initially launched on Base, the blockchain connected to Coinbase (NASDAQ: COIN), where Sentora reports a $1 million supply, but it is not yet available on Ethereum. These tokenized funds bring in modest revenue compared to JPMorgan’s core businesses. Fees from these funds contribute to Asset & Wealth Management, which manages over $5.1 trillion in client assets, while payments revenue, including JPMD, grew 12% in the second quarter. Additionally, neither Sentora nor JPMorgan has disclosed how JLTXX’s $792 million is split between Ethereum and Solana, making it hard to say Solana has a significant share. The announcements did not commit anyone to buy or hold ETH or SOL. When a tokenized fund moves its assets, it incurs small transaction fees known as gas. However, money market fund tokens mainly sit in a few institutional wallets, so they generate far less fee activity than stablecoin transfers or trading. The Solana announcement notably excluded details about the on-chain cash used to trade the fund tokens. It mentioned Morgan Money as the subscription channel but did not reference any stablecoin or JPMD for Solana. Until JPMorgan identifies an on-chain cash option for Solana, the bank’s own dollars will remain absent from that chain. When explaining its choice of Ethereum, JPMorgan cited its “established depth of on-chain liquidity and tokenized assets,” yet Sentora still shows no JPMD supply on Ethereum. Paul Przybylski, who leads digital and tokenized assets at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said clients operate across multiple networks, so their liquidity should reflect that need. However, he did not provide specific figures to back that demand. JPMorgan’s timing on Solana also could be considered late, as competitors like BlackRock (NYSE: BLK) and Franklin Templeton introduced tokenized funds there in 2025. Currently, the market appears to be contracting, with Sentora reporting $14.4 billion in tokenized Treasury and money market products across 119 offerings, a 3.5% decline over the past month. Ethereum currently leads JPMorgan’s tokenized funds. MONY’s $103.1 million is entirely Ethereum-based, JLTXX launched there first, and JPMD integrated into Ethereum before any other chain besides Base. Because Base is an Ethereum layer-2 network, the $1 million JPMD supply also links back to Ethereum. JPMorgan and the respective coins gain different advantages from this move. JPMorgan stands to benefit from fee-generating fund assets and a reserve product tailored for stablecoin issuers, while Ethereum and Solana gain enhanced credibility and the potential for increased stablecoin and trading activity stemming from involvement with a prominent bank like JPMorgan. While both networks use a portion of their fees for validator rewards, the flow is negligible at these fund sizes. For now, Ethereum appears to benefit more from JPMorgan’s tokenized funds, though neither asset has guaranteed buyers. ETH has declined 12.5% over the past month, while SOL’s value has fallen 16.1%, trends that far outweigh the impact of a few hundred million dollars in funds. Solana could gain ground if JPMorgan names it as a JPMD network, giving the funds an on-chain cash option there, or if a Solana-based stablecoin issuer starts holding its reserves in JLTXX. If JPMD’s Ethereum supply rises above zero before JPMorgan announces anything for Solana, Ethereum’s lead likely holds, but a Solana JPMD launch first could start shifting the advantage to SOL. title: Have Government Bond Yields Peaked? JPMorgan Sees Potential Support for Global Stocks - Yahoo Finance UK
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results JPMorgan strategists led by Mislav Matejka believe the recent rise in government bond yields may be losing momentum, potentially improving conditions for equity markets through the end of 2026. The bank previously identified signs that the increase in yields had become extended and that bonds were entering oversold territory. Its fixed income team's year-end forecasts for longer-dated yields across major markets are now broadly in line with or below prevailing levels. The outlook suggests that further substantial increases in borrowing costs are not central to JPMorgan's current market expectations. Higher government bond yields have contributed to declining equity valuation multiples by increasing the cost of capital and changing the relative returns available to investors. During the recent bond market selloff, forward price-to-earnings multiples fell by three points for the S&P 500 and MSCI All-Country World Equity Index. European equity multiples declined by approximately two points. JPMorgan believes the pressure on valuations could moderate if yields stop rising. "The multiple compression might not need to continue," the strategists said. The bank also expects more stable yields to ease concerns about consumer finances, the durability of the economic cycle and funding costs for AI-related investment. JPMorgan believes that most of the repricing associated with Federal Reserve interest rate expectations has already occurred. The strategists said changes in federal funds futures account for nearly all of the increase in the 10-year US Treasury yield this year. They do not anticipate substantial further adjustments to the market's expectations for US policy rates. Inflation expectations also remain contained, according to consumer surveys and financial market measures. Although recent US inflation figures have been elevated, JPMorgan estimates that underlying inflation is only around 0.3 percentage points above levels before the Iran war. European core inflation trends remain broadly similar to their pre-conflict levels, while wage growth and wage expectations remain subdued. JPMorgan does not expect borrowing by AI-related companies to materially reduce demand for government bonds. The bank also believes free cash flow at major hyperscale technology companies could prove better than current forecasts suggest. In Europe, the strategists identified France as an ongoing concern but did not consider a broader sovereign debt crisis their central scenario. They cited the European Central Bank's policy tools, stronger banking sector balance sheets, more diversified sovereign bond holdings and lower credit defaults than during the 2010–2012 eurozone debt crisis. These factors support JPMorgan's view that current financial risks may remain contained, although they have not been eliminated. JPMorgan described the early third-quarter earnings season as broadly supportive of equities. Among the first 29 US companies and 14 European companies to report, most exceeded earnings expectations and raised their guidance. The bank believes continued earnings growth, combined with stabilising bond yields, could help global stock markets recover from recent valuation pressure. Oil prices remain a source of uncertainty because of their potential effects on inflation and monetary policy expectations. Nevertheless, the strategists concluded that equities could perform positively through year-end if bond yields and corporate earnings develop in line with their forecasts. title: JPM Coin and USDC Follow Different Rules for Dollar Access - TOKENPOST
content: JPMD’s Ethereum transfers were limited to institutions approved by JPMorgan. Circle’s direct-redemption terms generally require an eligible Circle Mint account, with an exception for MiCAR-compliant redemptions. JPM Coin (JPMD) represents U.S. dollar deposits at JPMorgan and limits Ethereum transfers to approved institutions, while USD Coin (USDC) can move onchain without the same Circle Mint account requirement. The distinction involves both what each token represents and the rules for moving or redeeming it. JPMD represents customer deposits at JPMorgan. When the bank brought the token to Ethereum on Oct. 19, transfers were limited to institutions it approved. The bank’s approved-institution access model on Ethereum defines who can transfer JPMD on that network. USDC transfers onchain are separate from direct redemption. Receiving or transferring USDC does not by itself establish eligibility to redeem it directly for dollars. Direct dollar redemption through Circle requires a Circle Mint account. The two pathways serve different purposes: JPMD represents deposits held at a bank, while USDC is a dollar stablecoin with separate rules for direct redemption through its issuer. JPMorgan asset management analysts say so — and the firm projects it could surpass stocks, bonds and gold over the next decade. In a report published on Oct. 19, JPMorgan's asset management arm projected 10% annualized returns on Bitcoin over the next 10 years. By comparison, it projected 5.5% for gold, 5.6% for Treasury bonds and 7.5% for large-cap equities. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP JPMorgan's shift in tone is remarkable given the longstanding skepticism toward digital assets from its CEO Jamie Dimon. In 2017, he derided Bitcoin as a "fraud" heading toward a crash. He has kept up a barrage of criticism against Bitcoin, dismissing it as "a pet rock" and "worthless" over the years. Just last year, JPMorgan began allowing its clients to buy Bitcoin as banks developed a stronger interest in crypto. "I don't think you should smoke, but I defend your right to smoke," Dimon said during JPMorgan's annual investor day in May 2025. "I defend your right to buy bitcoin." However, the report offered a significant caveat for its projection: It still doesn't recommend Bitcoin as something that investors should purchase for a diversified portfolio. Bitcoin is a digital asset designed to be sent electronically between users anywhere in the world without a bank or government facilitating the transfer. Therefore, its value is not determined by a central government. It only stems from what an investor is prepared to pay. Bitcoin's volatility made JPMorgan analysts cautious about incorporating it in investment portfolios. "At the moment, we do not make a case for bitcoin (BTC) as a diversifier in portfolios due to its unstable market correlations," JPMorgan analysts Sheena Shah and Dennis Cristallo wrote in the analysis. "We see bitcoin as a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing." At its peak in October 2025, Bitcoin reached just over $126,000 in value. However, the digital token has swung wildly in value and shed a significant share of its worth since. Huge gains and sudden losses have dictated Bitcoin's trajectory since it was first launched in 2009. As of Oct. 23, it was trading at roughly $81,500 — down about 35% from its record high. Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors JPMorgan analysts observed that Bitcoin is "the anchor" of a crypto asset class now surpassing $2.5 trillion in value — about the size of the Swiss stock market and the burgeoning private capital market in the U.S., they wrote. "BTC mostly trades like a high beta risk asset that tracks global money supply growth, but it is sometimes treated as 'digital gold,'" the report said. Bitcoin's volatility is reflected in JPMorgan's forecast projections. It laid out a base case for roughly 10% returns over the next decade. The firm's "bear case" showed it could plunge about 10% in the same time frame. If Bitcoin had an extraordinary run, the firm's "bull case" said it could grow 17% in the next 10 years. Still, its status as a purely speculative investment led JPMorgan's asset management arm to consult against acquiring it. It was also cautious about projecting the trajectory of an asset that isn't anchored by traditional cash flow. "BTC currently lacks a clear role as a diversifier in balanced portfolios due to unstable correlations to other asset classes," JPMorgan analysts wrote. "Uncertain correlations, combined with high volatility, also limit its utility in strategic asset allocation today, in our view." title: JPMorgan Drops 'Bullish' Stance On US Stocks After Warsh's Hawkish Tone At Jackson Hole, Shifts To 'Tactically Cautious' - Stocktwits
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s trading team has stepped back from its bullish posture on U.S. equities, shifting to a tactically cautious stance ahead of the Federal Reserve’s upcoming policy decision. The recalibration follows recent hawkish remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, which prompted financial markets to price in an increased probability of interest-rate hikes before the end of the year. In a note to clients on Monday, accessed by Bloomberg, Andrew Tyler, head of U.S. market intelligence at JPMorgan, noted that while fundamental economic conditions and corporate earnings remain robust, short-term pressures are likely to cause stock indexes to move sideways rather than extend recent gains. Market sentiment shifted after Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech on Friday, which emphasized that inflation shows little sign of meaningfully cooling. Unlike past central bank leaders, Warsh has offered limited forward guidance regarding the magnitude and duration of potential rate increases. Tyler pointed out that if the central bank resumes raising borrowing costs, investors will face heightened uncertainty about the trajectory of monetary policy. Financial markets responded swiftly to the hawkish tone. The yield on the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury note climbed past 4.75% on Monday, hitting its highest level since January 2025. Meanwhile, interest-rate swap contracts signaled about a 70% probability that the Fed will implement a quarter-point rate increase next month, according to Bloomberg data. The CME FedWatch Tool on Monday indicated a 65.9% probability of a 25 basis point hike in the September rate-setting meeting, up from 57%. JPMorgan's tactical pivot comes as Wall Street enters September, traditionally the weakest calendar month for U.S. stock performance. Beyond monetary policy concerns, Tyler highlighted several near-term vulnerabilities for equity markets, including a cooling of momentum among high-valuation artificial intelligence stocks. Rising energy prices following recent military strikes between the U.S. and Iran and increased pressure on rate-sensitive utilities and defensive sectors. Despite these obstacles, broader market positioning remains largely balanced, and the S&P 500 Index was still on track to post an approximate 2.5% gain for August, while the Dow was set to end its fifth straight month in the green. Investors are now focused on incoming macroeconomic reports to gauge the Fed's next move. The upcoming monthly U.S. employment report, projected by economists to show an addition of 55,000 jobs in August, will serve as an initial indicator following July's unexpected contraction. "Equity bull markets tend to end with either a hiking cycle or a recession," Tyler wrote, reassuring investors that an economic contraction remains highly improbable in the near term. Nevertheless, he cautioned that the central bank’s forthcoming gathering has officially turned into a "live meeting." The SPDR S&P500 ETF (SPY), tech-heavy Invesco QQQ (QQQ), and the SPDR Dow Jones ETF (DIA) fell between 0.3% and 0.7% on Monday, with an overall ‘bullish’ retail sentiment. title: JPMorgan's JPM Coin Shows Zero Supply on Ethereum (ETH) After Oct. 19 Launch - Cryptonews.net
content: JPMorgan's deposit token has been live on Ethereum ($ETH) since Oct. 19, and the contract data so far reads a flat zero. As of Oct. 22, the Ethereum deployment of JPM Coin (JPMD) showed zero circulating supply and zero recorded transfers, with exactly one allowlisted address registered in the verified smart contract. The bank, whose shares trade under JPMorgan (JPM), opened the token to approved institutional clients on the network that day, extending a rollout that began in November 2025 on Base, Coinbase's Layer 2 network. The Base contract tells a quieter version of the same story: about 1,001,000 tokens held across two addresses, unchanged since Nov. 20, 2025. JPM Coin is a tokenized claim on dollar deposits held at the bank, and its structure differs from an open stablecoin: the contract sits on a public blockchain, but only approved customer addresses can receive the token. Sentora, the on-chain research firm behind the review published Oct. 23, notes that an address count measures registered addresses, not customers or actual users, and that a standing supply figure cannot capture payments where issuance and redemption happen within the same day. In plain terms, supply is the amount of a token outstanding at a given moment, so the zero balance describes the Ethereum ($ETH) contract's state on Oct. 22 rather than everything JPM Coin does across networks. The unchanged Base balance also does not rule out earlier transfers, since the review reports a snapshot rather than a full transfer history for that network. The Oct. 19 announcement cited Ethereum's tokenized asset and liquidity base as the reason for expansion, but an announcement and actual issuance are separate stages, and JPMorgan has not disclosed issuance or transaction volumes for the new deployment. The launch landed while Ethereum price discussion this week has centered on institutional flows rather than new rails. Sentora's published research adds the second data point, and this one shows movement. Its contract-level analysis put $400 million in redemptions on the Ethereum ($ETH) deployment of JLTXX, a tokenized money market fund from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, across Oct. 21 and Oct. 22. Over the same two days, the fund's Solana deployment climbed from effectively zero to $450 million. The pairing is suggestive rather than conclusive: one figure is a redemption flow, the other a standing deployment size, and the data does not tie individual investors to both sides of the move. The product context arrived on Oct. 22, when the asset manager announced that JLTXX and its My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) were open to qualified U.S. investors on Solana, with subscriptions and redemptions handled through the firm's Morgan Money platform. JLTXX is described in that announcement as a U.S. registered government money market fund built to support stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. “Our clients operate across more than one network, and their liquidity should too,” said Paul Przybylski, who leads product, digital and tokenized assets at the firm. MONY, a private placement launched in December 2025, carries a $1 million minimum, fees of 16 basis points, and a portfolio of U.S. Treasury securities and Treasury-backed repurchase agreements targeting a $1 net asset value per share outside Rule 2a-7. Investors need their own blockchain addresses to hold the tokens, peer-to-peer transfers are restricted to clients, and official shareholder records stay off-chain with SS&C as transfer agent. JPMorgan's materials also note that interests in the funds are not bank accounts and carry no Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insurance. The same briefing found no live on-chain integration connecting JPM Coin with the bank's funds or decentralized finance protocols. The two records read together sketch where institutional usage of Ethereum actually stands. On Sentora's published research, the primary document behind both stories, the newest institutional rail is live in name only four days after its announcement, while the fund flow data shows Ethereum holding a large tokenized money market footprint but ceding its fastest-growing leg to Solana. Neither point is, by itself, a verdict on Ethereum adoption: allowlisted deployments start slowly by design, and same-day issue-and-redeem payments would leave no trace in a standing balance. The markers worth tracking are specific: the first non-zero issuance or transfer on the Ethereum JPMD contract, and whether JLTXX's Ethereum deployment stabilizes once the Oct. 21–22 redemption window is behind it. Broader market pressure is a separate variable: spot ETF products logged a $110.6 million net outflow on Oct. 22, and the chart sits near the $2,300 support zone ahead of the Federal Reserve decision.

title: JPMorgan Expands Tokenized Money Market Funds To Solana - TradingView
content: TL;DR: J.P. Morgan Asset Management says qualified U.S. investors can now access MONY and JLTXX tokenized money market funds on Solana through its Morgan Money platform. J.P. Morgan Asset Management is bringing two of its tokenized money market funds to Solana, extending a traditional cash-management business across another public blockchain. In an announcement Thursday, the investment manager said qualified U.S. investors can now access My OnChain Net Yield Fund, known as MONY, and the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity–Token Money Market Fund, JLTXX, on Solana through its Morgan Money platform. Investors can subscribe and redeem through that institutional interface and receive balances represented at blockchain addresses. The two products are not identical forms of digital cash. MONY is a private placement offered under Rule 506(c), with eligibility restrictions for qualifying investors. JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund structured to serve cash management needs, including those of stablecoin issuers. Both represent fund interests rather than ordinary deposit balances. J.P. Morgan's disclosures make clear that the funds are not bank accounts or FDIC-insured deposits, and that even products seeking a stable $1 share value can lose money. That difference is easy to overlook when a token moves through a wallet interface. The blockchain record can make ownership and transfers more programmable; it does not change the underlying fund's investment objectives, regulatory status or redemption restrictions. Institutions experimenting with tokenized assets increasingly operate across more than one chain. A fund that can be subscribed into on multiple networks may be more useful as a liquidity-management instrument, particularly when portfolio and treasury teams hold digital balances in different environments. J.P. Morgan says adding Solana is intended to let clients access the same fund strategies across the networks where they operate. It is a distribution and settlement expansion, not the creation of two wholly new investment strategies. The bank's Morgan Money platform remains central to the customer experience. That is significant because professional investors need controls that go beyond seeing a token balance, including eligibility screening, reporting, fund documents and predictable subscriptions and redemptions. The company published Solana token addresses for both products, but copying a token identifier from social media is not a substitute for using the manager's verified onboarding channel. Token impersonation and lookalike assets remain a risk in on-chain markets. For Solana, the listing adds another institutional financial product beyond speculative trading. For J.P. Morgan, it tests whether a familiar regulated fund structure can retain its governance while using a wider set of blockchain rails. Actual institutional adoption and transaction volumes, not the announcement alone, will show the importance of that change. Source: www.prnewswire.com original announcement or data. Sentora’s subsequent review reported no issued supply or transfers in the Ethereum contract it examined. Its Base findings described an unchanged supply balance, with holdings concentrated in two addresses. An unchanged supply figure does not, by itself, establish whether transfers occurred during that period. Sentora’s briefing expressly reported zero transfers for Ethereum but did not provide an equivalent historical transfer count for Base. The firm further said it had found no live on-chain integration between JPM Coin and the bank’s money market funds or decentralized finance protocols. Its statement concerned the integrations visible in its review, without documenting every potential institutional arrangement. Sentora reported that JLTXX’s Ethereum deployment recorded $400 million in redemptions across Oct. 21–22. Over the same period, its briefing placed the Solana deployment at $450 million after starting near zero. The figures describe different measures across two networks. Morgan Asset Management announced on Oct. 22 that JLTXX and its My OnChain Net Yield Fund, known as MONY, were available to qualified U.S. investors on Solana. Investors can access the two tokenized funds through Morgan Money, which handles subscriptions and redemptions and delivers token balances to blockchain addresses. “Our clients operate across more than one network, and their liquidity should too,” said Paul Przybylski, the asset manager’s global head of product, digital and tokenized assets. The company’s announcement identifies JLTXX as a U.S. registered government money market fund designed to support stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. MONY is a separate private placement fund launched in December 2025. The release does not disclose assets held on Solana for either product. JPMorgan’s MONY FAQ lists a $1 million initial investment minimum and fees of 16 basis points. Although its guidelines follow those applicable to government money market funds, the private vehicle is not subject to Rule 2a-7. BNY said Citadel Securities purchased a two-year U.S. Treasury note through the bank on Tradeweb. A tokenized representation of the security settled within minutes on BNY’s private digital ledger before Citadel Securities pledged it as collateral in an overnight triparty repurchase agreement. BNY supplied cash against the security and described the transaction as the first use of tokenized assets on a major triparty repo platform. Its announcement documented trade execution, settlement and financing within the same workflow. The bank said it plans to introduce further digital cash and tokenized deposit services. BNY expects to expand operating hours for its traditional settlement platforms covering Fed-eligible securities and U.S. triparty transactions into European and Asian trading hours next year. title: Rockefeller Lands $4.8M J.P. Morgan Team in Houston, UBS Duo in Ohio - AdvisorHub
content: Rockefeller Global Family Office has hired a J.P. Morgan Wealth Management team in Houston that oversaw $700 million in client assets and a UBS Wealth Management USA team in Columbus, Ohio, that oversaw $350 million, according to a source familiar with the moves. The Houston team, Sage Wealth Partners, is led by Christopher D. Sheets and Forrest R. Green and produced $4.8 million in annual revenue, according to the source. At J.P. Morgan Advisors, the pair worked with a third partner, T. Scott Holstead, as SGH Group. Holstead, a founding member of the Houston wealth office, remained with J.P. Morgan, but the other nine members of the team—including Sheets’ son Cameron—made the move, a second source said. Sheets and Green joined J.P. Morgan in 2018. They began their advisory careers at Bernstein Private Wealth Management in 2002 and 2004, respectively, according to registration records. The UBS team, Shea Wealth Partners, is led by Andrea M. Shea and her son, Martin E. Shea, who produced $2.5 million in annual revenue, the source said. The four-person team worked out of UBS offices in the Columbus suburb of Upper Arlington and near Cleveland in Pepper Pike, Ohio, according to its UBS website, which was no longer online Friday afternoon. Andrea Shea joined UBS in 2009 after four years with Morgan Stanley predecessor Smith Barney, according to registration records. She began her career in 1998 and was registered with three brokerages through 2000. Martin Shea joined her at UBS in 2022. Spokespeople for J.P. Morgan and UBS did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Rockefeller opened an office in Columbus in August with Jones Wealth Partners, a team from Merrill Lynch, and also has offices in Cincinnati and Cleveland, the firm said at the time. In Houston, Rockefeller in April snagged a Merrill Lynch team producing $14 million in annual revenue. Rockefeller Capital Management, the parent of Rockefeller Global Family Office, reported overseeing $237 billion in client assets at the end of August. Earlier this month, the firm hired a $1.2 billion Truist team that joined an office in Naples, Florida, established five months earlier with the addition of a billion-dollar Morgan Stanley team. J.P. Morgan Advisors, the bank’s traditional brokerage unit, has around 600 advisors. Last week, two of the unit’s largest teams, led by Phil Scott and Jim Atwood, left to launch their own RIA with $18.6 billion in client assets and $130 million in combined annual revenue. J.P. Morgan Wealth Management had 6,433 advisors, including those in Chase bank branches, at the end of September, up 7% from a year earlier, according to its earnings report. UBS’s Americas wealth unit had 5,644 advisors at the end of June, down 2.2% from a year earlier. At least 54 teams with $51.8 billion in client assets left UBS for rivals in 2025, and at least 27 teams with $28 billion departed in the first half of this year. Shawn L. Bernhard had spent less than 18 months at Raymond James after a lengthy career at UBS.

title: Credit markets look for AI’s weak links - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has hit turbulence over the past few weeks. AI-related stocks have fallen much more sharply than the broader market as investors reconsider the financing costs of building data centers, buying chips and supplying the electricity needed to run them. Still, investors have seen rotations out of AI before. What makes this episode different is the simultaneous action in credit markets. The cost of insuring the debt of several AI-linked companies has reached record levels as the sector grows more reliant on debt financing. But rather than a blanket vote against the ecosystem, the rising cost of default protection reflects a targeted reassessment of repayment risk. In other words, credit markets are taking a hard look at the AI build-out and asking who can afford to keep at it. Credit default swaps (CDS) act like insurance on a company’s debt. CDS buyers pay a recurring premium and, if the borrower experiences a major credit event, such as bankruptcy or failure to pay, the buyer will receive a large payout. The premium is quoted in basis points. A CDS spread of 100 basis points broadly means that insuring $10 million of debt costs $100,000 per year. At 1,000 basis points, the annual cost rises to roughly $1 million.1 Credit default swaps can provide a measure of market sentiment. A wider CDS spread does not necessarily signal an expected failure. It can also reflect greater hedging demand, heavy debt issuance or uncertainty about future financing. The level, speed and confirmation from other markets help distinguish routine insurance from genuine distress. Credit spreads have widened over the past month, but technology-related borrowers have moved much more sharply than the broader investment grade market. The spread between the two has spiked higher than even during the tech-driven downturn of 2022. Going one level deeper, AI-related CDS have risen even more rapidly in the past month, but not all in parallel. For large, cash-generative AI leaders, five-year CDS spreads range from 50–120 basis points. These are elevated levels for companies with strong balance sheets, but they still look more like the price of portfolio insurance than a prediction of financial distress. These companies still have far lower leverage and higher interest coverage ratios than the average investment grade borrower. The picture changes as debt becomes more important to the business model. Default protection on some established investment grade infrastructure borrowers has climbed toward 300 basis points. That represents a meaningful reassessment of credit risk. At the weak end of the spectrum, one financing-dependent AI infrastructure borrower has taken on tens of billions of dollars in debt and other obligations. Its five-year CDS shot up to 1,100 basis points this week, so insuring $10 million of its debt would cost more than $1 million per year. Pricing at these levels implies near or above a 50% probability of default over five years, up from below 30% a year ago. That is not a forecast, but it is difficult to dismiss.2 Put together, investors are demanding roughly 10 times as much to insure the weakest AI borrower as the strongest companies in the ecosystem. Yet broad investment grade protection remains comparatively contained. If markets were losing confidence in corporate balance sheets generally, that would not be the case. The concern is confined to business models that require debt markets to remain open while spending stays high and cash flow remains limited. Lehman Brothers’ CDS averaged less than 100 basis points in the third quarter of 2007. By mid-September 2008, they had risen to over 1,400 and the firm had filed for bankruptcy. CDS did not predict the exact moment when Lehman would run out of options. But the steady rise in protection costs, reinforced by falling bond and equity prices and mounting funding pressure, clearly showed that the market was losing confidence in the firm’s ability to pay its debts. Not every warning ends the same way. In 2005, default protection on a major U.S. automaker rose sharply ahead of its downgrade to high yield. The company’s financial pressure was real, but it raised liquidity, restructured and avoided bankruptcy. That is how investors can view CDS today—as warning lights rather than countdown clocks. As long as broad investment grade spreads remain contained, and stronger borrowers retain access to capital, stress among the riskiest issuers is unlikely to derail the broader AI build-out. However, the AI label alone is no longer enough to reassure lenders. Companies must show that they can finance investment, service their debt and eventually turn spending into cash flow. Credit markets are scrutinizing the AI build-out and deciding who is financially equipped to finish it.
